questionText: State two causes of protein denaturation and give one example in each case.

rows.verbatim: State two causes of protein denaturation and give one example in each case.
rows.contextNote: Any TWO of the five causes the scheme lists, each with an example. One option is worth 3 marks: 2 for the cause (graded 2:0) and 1 for the example (graded 1:0) — both all-or-nothing, so a correct cause with no example or a wrong example still scores 2 of the 3. In the scheme's table the mechanical-action cause cell also carries "e.g whisking, beating", and acids, enzymes and salt all sit under the heading "Chemicals: such as", so the chemical must be named rather than left as "chemicals".

options: Heat Hard boiled eggs; omelette; quiche; egg custard; dry heat causes meat to shrink; collagen changes to gelatine in meat; browning of meat; etc.
Mechanical action Sponge cake; soufflés; meringues; etc
Acids Cheese-making; vinegar in marinade tenderises meat; sour milk lactose changes to lactic acid etc.
Enzymes Rennin coagulates casein in the stomach; cheese-making; tenderising meat etc.

notes: Section A questions are 6 marks each; here that is 2 causes @ 2 marks + 2 examples @ 1 mark. Modelled as best 2 of the 5 causes the scheme lists (heat, mechanical action, acids, enzymes, salt), with each option carrying its own example column so the pairing is preserved — an example that does not belong to the named cause cannot earn the second mark. Options are the scheme's own table rows. openList true: three of the five example lists close with "etc.", so other correct examples score.

questionText: In relation to lipids, explain each of the following: (i) Oxidative rancidity (ii) Hydrolytic rancidity

rows.verbatim: This occurs as a result of a reaction which takes place between unsaturated fatty acids and oxygen in the air; oxygen combines with the carbon atoms at the double bond; causes unpleasant rancid smell due to the production of compounds i.e. aldehydes and ketones; etc.
rows.contextNote: Part (i) Oxidative rancidity. This is ONE graded point worth 3 marks (graded 3:2:1:0) — the semicolons separate elements of the same explanation, not separate marks. A full explanation naming the reaction between unsaturated fatty acids and oxygen scores 3; a thinner or partly correct explanation is graded down to 2 or 1.

rows.verbatim: This occurs when enzymes (lipases) hydrolyse fats; breaking them down into fatty acids and glycerol; micro-organisms (bacteria) present in fat foods may also produce enzymes which hydrolyse fats; can give an unpleasant taste and smell; occurs in freezers when enzymes are not destroyed; etc.
rows.contextNote: Part (ii) Hydrolytic rancidity. Again ONE graded point worth 3 marks (graded 3:2:1:0): naming enzyme (lipase) hydrolysis of fats into fatty acids and glycerol earns the full 3, a partial explanation is graded down.

notes: Both terms are named in the question and each is priced at 3 marks, so this is fixed (3 + 3 = 6), not a choice. The 3:2:1:0 band is a sliding value for one point per part, so each part is modelled as a single row at its full value with the grading explained in contextNote rather than split into three 1-mark rows. openList true: both explanations close with "etc."

rows.contextNote: Iodine — name any ONE of these conditions. Graded 2:0, all-or-nothing.

rows.contextNote: The definition is ONE graded point worth 4 marks (graded 4:3:2:1:0) — the semicolons are elements of a single explanation, not four separate marks. "The minimum amount of energy needed to sustain the body at complete rest" is the core; adding what that energy is used for (body temperature, internal organs) is what carries a thin answer up to the full 4.

rows.verbatim: Give two factors that determine a person’s basal metabolic rate.
rows.contextNote: Any TWO factors, 1 mark each (graded 1:0, all-or-nothing per factor). The scheme's split of these into (i) and (ii) is only its line layout — the two lines are one pool, so any two of the factors below score.

notes: Two separately priced components — the definition at 4 marks and two factors at 1 mark each — so fixed, 4 + 1 + 1 = 6. The 4:3:2:1:0 band is a sliding value for the one definition point, modelled as a single 4-mark row. The factors are pooled into one any-2 row because the scheme's (i)/(ii) labels merely wrap the list across two lines; there is no requirement that one factor comes from each line. openList true: both the definition and the factor list close with "etc."

questionText: Explain each of the following chemical changes that occur during food preparation/cooking: Enzymic browning; Non-enzymic browning.

rows.verbatim: Enzymic browning — When fruit/vegetables are cut or damaged the cells release an enzyme, oxidase; which reacts with the oxygen in the air causing oxidation; as a result the food changes colour, e.g. apples turn brown
rows.contextNote: One graded point of 3 (3:2:1:0), not three separate ticks: the fuller the explanation — enzyme released, reaction with oxygen, resulting colour change — the higher the band, and a bare 'the food goes brown' sits at the bottom of it.

rows.verbatim: Non-enzymic browning — any one of the following explained
rows.contextNote: The second graded point of 3 (3:2:1:0). One of these three explained fully earns the 3; naming the reaction without explaining it sits lower in the band.

options: Maillard reaction - browning which occurs when amino acids and carbohydrates react when heated
Caramelisation – sugar melts and changes to a brown syrup / caramel
Dextrinisation – dextrins, short chains of polysaccharides form on carbohydrate foods in dry heat causing browning e.g. toast

notes: Section A Q9, 6 marks: '2 @ 3marks (graded 3:2:1:0)' — one point for enzymic browning and one for non-enzymic, so fixed with two rows of 3. Enzymic browning is one connected explanation in the scheme, so it is one row quoted whole; non-enzymic browning is printed as three alternative reactions (Maillard, caramelisation, dextrinisation) and the candidate explains one, so that half is a pick-one menu. Both graded bands are described in the context notes rather than split into invented sub-marks. openList true on both — the scheme ends both blocks with 'etc.'. No stem and no figure.

Structure and example stay separate rows within each card because they are graded differently -- a student who describes the chain perfectly and names no acid still loses 2 of the 6. he-2025-hl-sb-q1b keeps its id, as the saturated card, so no card id vanishes from the deck.

questionText: Discuss the significance of fatty acids in the diet.

rows.verbatim: Discuss the significance of fatty acids in the diet
rows.contextNote: Three points at 4 marks, graded 4:3:2:1:0 — again a ladder, so depth inside a point is paid for. "Discuss" is doing work here: the scheme's own entries pair a fatty acid with what it does to the body, and a point that names the acid without saying what it does sits at the bottom of the ladder. Note the two directions on offer — some of these are benefits and some are risks, and both count.

options: Essential fatty acids linoleic, linolenic and arachidonic – cannot be manufactured by the body so must be obtained from food; component of cell membranes; make hormones that regulate the immune system and central nervous system; brain development/functioning/cognitive functions; may help reduce LDL cholesterol and increase HDL cholesterol; etc.

temporary emulsion e.g. French dressing; etc.

questionText: Analyse the factors that impact the food choices and eating habits of adults in Ireland.

Naming eight factors and analysing none scores 12 of 20.

questionText: Describe three main functions of the family in contemporary society and outline how the State supports the family with each of these functions.

rows.verbatim: Describe three main functions of the family and outline how the State supports each
rows.contextNote: Three functions at 6 marks, graded in single steps all the way from 6 to 0 — the most forgiving ladder on the paper, and the one where detail is most directly paid for. Physical function provides for the basic physical needs; etc. State support social welfare payments; free G.P. care; school meals; etc.

stir high risk liquid foods i.e. stew and gravy to ensure they are re-heated throughout

options: store raw meat/poultry under/away from cooked produce

cool and fast freeze prepared foods immediately

These are ordered processes and the scheme lists them in sequence: for jam, sterilising the jars comes before the fruit and setting point before potting. A step out of order describes a process that would not work.

options: jam/chutney making: wash jars; sterilise jars; prepare fruit and vegetables according to type; use heavy based saucepan; simmer fruit to release pectin; add sugar; lemon juice can be added to increase acidity; boil until setting point is reached; test; skim; pot; seal; label; store; etc.
bottling/aseptic canning/in container canning: heat jars/cans of fruit/vegetables in a water bath; seal jars/cans when hot; forms a vacuum on cooling that creates a seal; label; store; etc.
drying: tie herbs into bundles; dry in a warm area; package; label; store; etc.
freezing: blanch according to type; put into moisture proof packaging; remove air; seal; label; freeze at -25˚C; store -18˚C; etc.
commercial freezing: flow; cryogenic; immersion; plate; blast; etc.
commercial drying: sun; hot air; roller; spray; AFD; etc.

notes: 25 marks split 5 + 20. Kept as two rows because the naming mark is priced separately and is the single cheapest mark in Section B.

questionText: Using the information provided in the chart, comment and elaborate on four factors that affect consumer decisions when purchasing food.
stem: The Eurobarometer survey 2022 and 2019 questioned consumers on factors that affect their decisions when purchasing foods. (adapted from www.efsa.europa.eu)

rows.verbatim: Comment and elaborate on four factors that affect consumer decisions when purchasing food
rows.contextNote: Four of the five factors the chart plots, 5 marks each on a full 5:4:3:2:1:0 ladder — depth is paid for a mark at a time, so this rewards saying more about fewer things. Each option opens with the chart's own movement since 2019 (cost up, environment sharply up, origin down, nutrient content flat), and quoting that direction is the cheapest mark on the question. "Comment and elaborate" then wants the why behind the movement.

options: Cost increased since 2019; increase in cost of living; inflation; increase in food transport costs; increased tariffs on imported food products; current conflicts in the world; increasing raw ingredients/materials cost; increase in energy costs; food shortages; sugar tax; etc.

Food safety slight increase since 2019; food poisoning bacteria; additives; pesticide residue; antibiotic; hormone; steroid residue; genetically modified foods; foods containing animal diseases; microplastics; antibiotic resistant bacteria in foods; etc.

Origin of food decrease since 2019; food traceability; rules governing food production in different countries; food miles; geographical location; cultural background; marketing strategies used by food establishments; food safety agencies; etc.

Impact on environment huge increase since 2019; food miles; amount of water used; amount and type of energy used during production; amount of CO2 produced; methane gas produced; pollution of water; air; soil; depletion of nutrients from soil; organic foods; pesticides used; food waste; transport; seasonal foods; type of packaging used; etc.

Nutrient content no change since 2019; meeting RDA for different nutrients; age of person; health status of person; hobbies and activities; dietary advice; advertising; social media; influencers; etc.

notes: Five factors on the chart, best four taken. Each option keeps its 2019 trend because the question says "using the information provided in the chart" — an answer that never touches the data is answering a different question.

questionText: Give a detailed account of carbohydrates and refer to: basic structure of a monosaccharide; formation of disaccharides; biological functions.
stem: The Eurobarometer survey 2022 and 2019 questioned consumers on factors that affect their decisions when purchasing foods. (adapted from www.efsa.europa.eu)

tariffModel.notation: monosaccharide structure 1 point @ 8 marks (graded 8:7:6:5:4:3:2:1:0); disaccharide formation 4 points @ 2 marks (graded 2:1:0); biological functions 3 points @ 2 marks (graded 2:1:0)

rows.contextNote: One point worth 8 marks, on a ladder that runs the whole way from 8 to 0 — the single most valuable marking point in Section B, and it is worth writing everything you know. The formula, the ring, the single sugar unit and a named example are four separate things the marker can climb; a labelled diagram earns here too.

Four points at 2 marks. The condensation reaction is the point students most often half-make: two monosaccharides joining is 1, and the water molecule eliminated is what earns the second. The formula C12H22O11 is a free 2 marks.

options: with the lost/elimination of one water molecule, condensation reaction

rows.contextNote: Three functions at 2 marks. Half this list is fibre rather than sugar — bowel movements, cholesterol, satiety — and fibre functions count, which is what makes this the easiest of the three strands to fill.

options: spares protein for primary function of growth
excess sugar/starch converted into adipose tissue
fibre allows for regular bowel movements
slow release of glucose into bloodstream
absorbs water and swells, delaying feeling of hungry

notes: 22 marks split 8 + 8 + 6 across the question's own three bullets. The 8-mark single point is unusual and is why the strands are separate rows rather than a pooled list.

questionText: Describe three properties of sugar and give one culinary example of each property.
stem: The Eurobarometer survey 2022 and 2019 questioned consumers on factors that affect their decisions when purchasing foods. (adapted from www.efsa.europa.eu)

tariffModel.notation: 3 properties @ 6 marks (graded 6:5:4:3:2:1:0); [name 2 marks (graded 2:0), description 2 marks (graded 2:1:0), culinary application 2 marks (graded 2:1:0)] x3

rows.verbatim: Describe three properties of sugar and give one culinary example of each property
rows.contextNote: Three properties at 6 marks, and each 6 splits three ways: 2 for naming the property, 2 for describing it, 2 for a culinary application. That last 2 is the one most often dropped — a perfect description of caramelisation with no crème brûlée against it scores 4 of 6. Each option below carries its own culinary application for that reason; an example borrowed from another property does not pay.

options: solubility sugars are white crystalline compounds, soluble in water; solubility is increased by heating water; a syrup is formed when sugar and water are heated; etc. culinary application icing; syrup; canned/bottled fruit; beverages; etc.

sweetness sugar has varying degrees of sweetness based on a point scale using the tasting method; sucrose has a relative sweetness of 100; glucose has a relative sweetness of 75; fructose has a relative sweetness of 170; lactose has a relative sweetness of 15; etc. culinary application cakes; sweets; shortbread; beverages; etc.
assists aeration sugar denatures egg protein, enabling aeration to occur; egg when whisked with sugar becomes aerated; etc. culinary application sponge cake; meringues; etc.

Maillard reaction non enzymic reaction between sugar (carbohydrates) and amino acids (proteins) in dry heat, causing brown colour to develop; etc. culinary application roast potatoes; roast meat; shortbread; buns; cakes; etc.

caramelisation when sugar is heated, it melts and produces caramel; there are 10 gradual changes in sugar between melting and caramelisation; these stages occur between 104oC and 177oC; eventually the heat will cause carbonisation (burning) of the sugar; etc. culinary application crème caramel; crème brûlée; caramel; etc.

crystallisation occurs when too much sugar is added to a mixture/liquid; mixture/liquid absorbs as much sugar as it can; crystal particles form when mixture cools; etc. culinary application hard sweets; confectionery; etc.

hydrolysis and inversion disaccharide sugars react with water and enzymes breaking down into monosaccharides; inversion is caused by heating sugar with an acid or by adding an enzyme; sucrose breaks down into glucose and fructose, known as invert sugar; etc. culinary application sweets; jam; etc.

notes: Seven properties in the scheme, best three taken, each kept with its own culinary-application line because the scheme pairs them and marks them together.

questionText: Discuss the dietary guidelines to follow when planning and preparing meals for a woman during pregnancy.
stem: 'A foetus is dependent on its mother for nutrition; so pregnant women must eat healthily and safely.' (www.bordbia.ie)

rows.verbatim: Discuss the dietary guidelines to follow when planning and preparing meals for a woman during pregnancy
rows.contextNote: Five guidelines at 4 marks, graded 4:2:0 — named is 2, discussed is 4, nothing between. The scheme's list runs in two directions, include and avoid, and both count: the avoid side (pâté, soft ripened cheese, unpasteurised dairy, shellfish, undercooked meat) is about listeria and is the half students forget. A nutrient named without saying what it does for the pregnancy stays at 2.

options: use of food pyramid for nutritional balance
energy balance vis a vis activity levels and stage of pregnancy

notes: The scheme prints far more than the 14 a card may show, so the list is taken in scheme order to the cap; the row stays openList, so any correct guideline still scores.

questionText: Give an account of Folic Acid/Folate under each of the following headings: sources; biological functions; properties.
stem: 'A foetus is dependent on its mother for nutrition; so pregnant women must eat healthily and safely.' (www.bordbia.ie)

tariffModel.notation: sources 3 @ 2 marks (graded 2:0); biological functions 3 @ 2 marks (graded 2:1:0); properties 3 @ 2 marks (graded 2:0)

rows.contextNote: Three sources at 2 marks, all-or-nothing (2:0). Nothing to describe — a correct food scores, a wrong one does not. Fortified cereals and supplements are on the list and are the two most often forgotten.

Three functions at 2 marks, and this one is graded 2:1:0 rather than 2:0 — the only strand of the three where a half-made point earns something. Neural tube defects is the function to lead with in a pregnancy question.

options: essential for synthesis and repair of DNA and RNA
development of brain, spinal cord and skeleton in foetus
reduces risk of neural tube defects

rows.contextNote: Three properties at 2 marks, all-or-nothing again. Properties are physical and chemical behaviour — solubility, heat stability, what destroys it — not what it does in the body. Mixing functions in here answers the previous bullet twice.

options: heat stable but some loss during cooking

notes: Three headings priced identically at 6 marks each. Worth showing the grading differences: two strands are all-or-nothing and the middle one is not.

questionText: Evaluate food labelling as a source of consumer information when purchasing foods for individuals with specific dietary requirements.
stem: 'A foetus is dependent on its mother for nutrition; so pregnant women must eat healthily and safely.' (www.bordbia.ie)

rows.verbatim: Evaluate food labelling as a source of consumer information
rows.contextNote: Three points at 4 marks, graded 4:2:0. The question says "for individuals with specific dietary requirements", so the allergen points do the most work — declared allergens, printed in bold — followed by the quantity declarations someone on a restricted diet actually reads. Listing label contents earns 2; saying what that content lets a particular consumer decide earns 4.

options: ingredients in descending order of weight

notes: The scheme prints one flat list of label contents, taken in order to the cap.

questionText: Discuss the changes that have evolved in Irish food and eating patterns in recent years.
stem: 'Artisan producers have altered Irish food culture to enrich our culinary heritage.' (Irish Examiner Jan. 2023)

rows.verbatim: Discuss the changes that have evolved in Irish food and eating patterns in recent years
rows.contextNote: Five changes at 4 marks, graded 4:2:0. The list is deliberately two-sided — convenience foods, salt, sugar and low fibre on one hand; wider choice, more nutritional knowledge and a focus on gut and mental health on the other — and an answer that runs only the decline story is telling half of it. Naming a change is 2; saying what drove it or what it costs is 4.

notes: One flat list, taken in scheme order to the cap.

questionText: Outline the stages involved in the manufacture of yogurt. In your answer refer to production, packaging and labelling.
stem: 'Artisan producers have altered Irish food culture to enrich our culinary heritage.' (Irish Examiner Jan. 2023)

rows.verbatim: Outline the stages involved in the manufacture of yogurt
rows.contextNote: Ten points at 2 marks — the highest point-count in Section B, and the one question where breadth beats depth outright. It is a sequence, and the temperatures are marking content: pasteurised at 80-90C, cooled to 37C for the culture, incubated 6-8 hours, cooled to 5C. A stage named without its temperature sits at 1. Packaging and labelling are named in the question and are the last two stages, so an account that stops at the finished yogurt leaves 4 marks behind.

options: starter culture of lactic acid bacteria/lactobacillus bulgaricus

notes: One ordered process. Kept as a single group because every stage is priced the same and the order is what carries the meaning.

questionText: Describe the protection provided to the consumer by the Food Hygiene Regulations 1950-1989.
stem: 'Artisan producers have altered Irish food culture to enrich our culinary heritage.' (Irish Examiner Jan. 2023)

rows.verbatim: Describe the protection provided to the consumer by the Food Hygiene Regulations 1950-1989
rows.contextNote: Only two points, at 5 marks each, so both must be developed — this is not a list. Graded 5:3:0: naming a provision is 3 and describing what it means in a food premises is 5. The enforcement point (closure orders, unfit food seized and destroyed) is the strongest one to take, because it describes itself.

options: prohibits sale of food that is diseased, contaminated or unfit for human consumption
precautions must be taken at each stage of production to prevent contamination of food
food premises must be registered and maintain hygienic conditions with regard to equipment, food waste, water supply
all food handlers must observe high standards of hygiene and follow Hazard Analysis Critical Control Point (HACCP) system
mobile food stalls where food is prepared and/or cooked/heated must apply for annual licence
if regulations are not followed, closure orders can be issued and unfit food be seized and destroyed

notes: One flat list; each entry is already a full provision, which suits a 5-mark point.

questionText: Analyse the changes in consumer shopping patterns over the last decade.
stem: 'Helpful, knowledgeable staff are the driving force behind in-store shopping being popular amongst Irish consumers.' (www.pwc.ie)

rows.verbatim: Analyse the changes in consumer shopping patterns over the last decade
rows.contextNote: Five changes at 4 marks, graded 4:2:0. "Analyse" is the difference between the 2 and the 4: self-service checkouts is a 2, and what they changed for the consumer and the retailer is the 4. The list splits into how people pay, how they shop, and what they value — spreading five points across all three reads better than five variations on technology.

options: TV, online and social media shopping

notes: One flat list, taken in scheme order to the cap.

questionText: Describe the protection provided to the consumer by the Consumer Protection Act 2007.
stem: 'Helpful, knowledgeable staff are the driving force behind in-store shopping being popular amongst Irish consumers.' (www.pwc.ie)

rows.verbatim: Describe the protection provided to the consumer by the Consumer Protection Act 2007
rows.contextNote: Three points at 4 marks, graded 4:2:0. The scheme's list is narrow and all of one shape — false or misleading claims about goods, services, price, previous price, recommended retail price — so the three points come from naming which claim, and the 4 comes from an example of what that misleading claim looks like in a shop.

options: false or misleading claims about goods
false or misleading claims about services
false or misleading claims about price

notes: One flat list. Short by design: this Act is examined on misleading claims rather than on redress, which belongs to the Sale of Goods Act.

questionText: Discuss the role of the family in meeting the physical and psychological needs of young children so that they will become well-adjusted adults in society.
stem: 'The family is a dynamic, fluid, resilient and ever changing fundamental institution of society.' (Kristy Hawthorn)

tariffModel.notation: 4 points @ 5 marks (graded 5:3:1:0); 1 point relating to physical, 1 point relating to psychological & 2 other points

rows.verbatim: Discuss the role of the family in meeting the physical and psychological needs of young children
rows.contextNote: Four points at 5 marks on a 5:3:1:0 ladder, and the distribution is fixed: at least one physical need, at least one psychological, then two of either. Four points on food and clothing cannot score 20 because a psychological mark is reserved. The question ends "so that they will become well-adjusted adults", and that clause is what lifts a 3 to a 5 — say what the need does for the adult the child becomes.

options: food parents to provide children with a healthy balanced diet; pay attention to nutritional requirements of the child; take responsibility for limiting the child’s intake of unhealthy food; etc.
clothing parents provide sufficient clothing for modesty and protection of the child; etc.
shelter children need shelter, a warm home in which to live, rest and play; etc. psychological
love affection that is experienced by the child in a relationship will allow the child to transfer this to his/her own relationships; etc.
security and trust the presence of a dependable, constant caregiver in a nurturing role will provide children with security and trust; etc.
praise and encouragement help to provide a stable and happy home life for children; promote self- esteem in the child; etc.
protection from physical, emotional and sexual abuse; etc.

notes: Physical needs (food, clothing, shelter) and psychological needs (love, security and trust, praise, protection) as the scheme groups them, with the reservation carried in the notation.

questionText: Analyse the impact of social, economic and technological changes on contemporary family structures.
stem: 'The family is a dynamic, fluid, resilient and ever changing fundamental institution of society.' (Kristy Hawthorn)

tariffModel.notation: 3 points @ 6 marks (graded 6:4:2:0); 1 point relating to social, economic & technological changes

rows.verbatim: Analyse the impact of social, economic and technological changes on contemporary family structures
rows.contextNote: Three points at 6 marks, one from each of the three named strands — the distribution here is total, not partial: there is no free point, so an answer missing any one strand caps at 12. Graded 6:4:2:0, and "analyse the impact" is the whole ladder: the change itself is the 2, and what it did to family structure is the 6.

options: social decline in extended family structure; increase in cohabitation; urbanisation; gender equality; dual career families; fewer children; women having children later in life; marital breakdown; separation and divorce; same sex marriage; adoption; surrogacy; family planning options; multi-cultural society; value of education; shared roles in home; stay at home fathers; increased leisure time; antisocial behaviour; etc.

economic increased cost of living/inflation; state benefits; both partners/parents working; higher standard of living; hybrid working; childcare availability and cost; cost of education and accommodation; demand for housing; moving from urban areas due to cost of housing; one parent working abroad; etc.

questionText: Describe two supports available to older family members and state how these supports help them to maintain their independence.
stem: 'The family is a dynamic, fluid, resilient and ever changing fundamental institution of society.' (Kristy Hawthorn)

rows.verbatim: Describe two supports available to older family members and state how these supports help them to maintain their independence
rows.contextNote: Two supports at 6 marks each — a short answer where both points must be developed twice over, because the question asks for the support AND how it maintains independence. Naming Meals on Wheels is the 2; describing it is the 4; saying that it lets someone stay in their own home is the 6. The named services (Meals on Wheels, Age Action, public health nurses, Home Support Services) are worth more than the generic ones.

options: voluntary services e.g. Meals on Wheels, Age Action
community care services e.g. public health nurses, Home Support Services

notes: One flat list of supports; the independence half of the question is not a separate scheme list, so it lives in the contextNote as the thing the second half of each 6 pays for.

questionText: Using the information presented in the table, discuss five factors that affect a person’s food choices.
stem: 'All around the world, people choose to eat different food for many different reasons.' (www.foodfactoflife.org.uk) The diagram lists factors affecting food choice: work patterns, food availability, emotions, likes and dislikes, cooking skills, money, time.

rows.verbatim: Discuss five factors that affect a person’s food choices
rows.contextNote: Five of the seven factors in the diagram, 4 marks each, graded 4:2:0 — named is 2, discussed is 4, nothing in between. Time and work patterns overlap heavily; taking both and saying the same thing about convenience food twice earns one 4, not two.

Time: busy lifestyle; use of convenience foods; take away foods; type of work; hours worked; etc.

Likes and dislikes may have a preference for foods high in sugar; may take a dislike to food due to allergies; appeals to senses; etc.

questionText: Give an account of carbohydrates under each of the following headings: classification; functions in the body; dietary sources.
stem: 'All around the world, people choose to eat different food for many different reasons.' (www.foodfactoflife.org.uk) The diagram lists factors affecting food choice: work patterns, food availability, emotions, likes and dislikes, cooking skills, money, time.

tariffModel.notation: classification 3 classes @ 2 marks (graded 2:0); functions 2 @ 5 marks (graded 5:3:0); sources 3 @ 4 marks (graded 4:2:0)

rows.contextNote: Three classes at 2 marks, all-or-nothing. The cheapest 6 marks in Section B: three words. Either the chemical names (mono-, di-, polysaccharides) or the everyday ones (sugar, starch, fibre) score.

Only two functions but 5 marks each — the opposite shape to the rest of this question, and the strand where a one-word answer costs most. Graded 5:3:0, so "energy" is a 3 and saying what the body does with it is the 5.

options: insulation, excess carbohydrate stored as adipose tissue
fibre gives a feeling of fullness

rows.contextNote: Three sources at 4 marks. Worth noticing this is the biggest strand of the three at 12 marks — more than classification and worth naming a food and saying which carbohydrate it provides, since the 2 is for the food and the other 2 for the link.

questionText: Outline three different ways a person can increase the amount of fibre in their diet.

use brown flour instead of white flour

questionText: Describe four ways consumers can reduce food waste when planning meals and purchasing foods.
stem: 'All around the world, people choose to eat different food for many different reasons.' (www.foodfactoflife.org.uk) The diagram lists factors affecting food choice: work patterns, food availability, emotions, likes and dislikes, cooking skills, money, time.

tariffModel.notation: 4 ways @ 5 marks (graded 5:4:3:0); 1 reference to planning, 1 reference to purchasing, & 2 other points

rows.verbatim: Describe four ways consumers can reduce food waste when planning meals and purchasing foods

questionText: Describe four factors that influence consumers when purchasing goods and services.

questionText: Give an account of the Small Claims Court procedure used to resolve a consumer dispute over goods or services.
stem: 'From time-to-time problems will arise with goods and services.' (www.ccpc.ie)

rows.verbatim: Give an account of the Small Claims Court procedure
rows.contextNote: Four points at 5 marks. This is a procedure with numbers in it, and the numbers are marking content: EUR 25 to process the form, 15 days for the respondent to reply, 28 days to comply with a judgment, claims up to EUR 2,000. questionText: Set out details of an alternative protein food you have studied. Refer to: name; stages in manufacture.
stem: Vegan diets are increasing in popularity; however, these diets require careful planning.

tariffModel.notation: name 2 marks (graded 2:0); stages in manufacture 6 points @ 3 marks (graded 3:2:0)

rows.verbatim: Name an alternative protein food and set out its stages of manufacture
rows.contextNote: ONE alternative protein food, worth 20 marks: 2 for naming it and 6 stages at 3. Pick one and stay in it — the scheme prices seven separate processes and stages cannot be mixed between them. Each is an ordered sequence and every one of them ends the same way, packaged and labelled, which are two of the six stages and the two most often left off.

options: Textured Vegetable Protein soya beans are cleaned and prepared; oil extracted; ground into flour; addition of ingredients; extruded and shaped; cooked and dried; packaged; labelled; etc.

Mycoprotein fungi are fermented; addition of ingredients; harvested, purified and dried; bound; addition of additives; textured and shaped; steamed; shaped into products/quorn; packaged; labelled; etc.
Tofu soya milk is curdled; the curds are pressed into blocks; soft cheese-like texture formed; can be smoked; packaged; labelled; etc.

Soya milk soya beans are cleaned; soaked in water; ground with soaking water; the mixture is heated; filtered; flavoured; may be homogenised; pasteurised, sterilised or dried; packaged; labelled; etc.

Soya yoghurt non-dairy bacteria culture is added to soya milk; mixed; sugar may be added; mixture is warmed to 30oC to 40oC; mixture is transferred to a thermos flask or electric yoghurt maker; incubated for 12 hours to ferment; fruit may be added; additives; packaged; labelled; etc.
Tempeh soya beans are cleaned, cooked and dehulled; infused with mould spores; packed into containers; heated to 30oC; left to ferment for 24 hours; packaged; labelled; etc.
Miso soya beans are cleaned; inoculated with a mould; water and salt are added; rice or barley may also be added; allowed to ferment; paste formed; packaged; labelled; etc.

notes: Seven foods in the scheme, one chosen; each kept whole because its stages belong to it. The naming mark is carried in the notation.

questionText: Describe the legal obligations for marriage in Ireland.

options: Over 18: both partners must be over 18 years of age; etc.

Mental capacity: both partners must have the mental capacity to understand the nature of marriage; this may not be present if either party is intoxicated, mentally impaired due to drugs or mentally ill; etc.
Notification: three months’ notice given to church for a religious ceremony; to a registrar for a civil marriage ceremony; etc.
Registered venue: ceremonies must take place in registered building; etc.
Free to marry: neither spouse may be in an existing marriage; both parties must be single, widowed or divorced; etc.
Voluntary basis: both partners cannot be forced to marry against their wishes; etc.
Wedding registration: marriages must be registered after ceremony; etc
Not closely related: partners must not be close blood relatives; must not be closely related through marriage; etc.

questionText: Identify and explain two factors which affect the absorption of iron in the body.
stem: The infographic shows two influencing factors on evening meal consumption: Health and Wellbeing (42%) and Responsible Living (27%). (What Ireland Ate Last Night Report 2020, Bord Bia Thinking House)

rows.verbatim: Identify and explain two factors which affect the absorption of iron in the body
rows.contextNote: Only two factors, but on a full 5-to-0 ladder — every mark is earned separately, so this is the part of Q1 where chemistry pays. The scheme's explanations are at a level most answers never reach: Vitamin C chemically changes non-haem iron to the more absorbable form, sulphur-containing amino acids convert ferric (Fe3+) to ferrous (Fe2+), tannins bind to iron. Naming a factor is 1 or 2; the mechanism is the rest.

options: Vitamin C – consuming food high in vitamin C chemically changes non- haem iron to the more easily absorbed haem iron; consuming - non- haem iron and haem iron foods together increases non-haem iron absorption; acidity – e.g. hydrochloric acid and citric acids, as the low pH helps to liberate iron from organic combinations making absorption easier; protein – sulphur-containing amino acids change iron from ferric form (Fe3+) to ferrous form (Fe2+); sugar – fructose aids the absorption of non-haem iron; etc.

oxalic acid; phytic acid; fibre intake of 35g or more per day; caffeine, tannins - bind to iron inhibiting absorption; lack of vitamin C – iron remains in non-haem form which is more difficult to absorb; excess alcohol - heavy alcohol consumption effects iron metabolism; smoking – cigarette smoke particles alter iron homeostasis; etc.

notes: The scheme's two groups, assisting and inhibiting, kept whole because each carries its own mechanism and the mechanism is where the marks are.

questionText: Differentiate between infectious food poisoning and toxic food poisoning.
stem: Temperature control is critical to ensuring food safety for all consumers.

rows.verbatim: Differentiate between infectious food poisoning and toxic food poisoning
rows.contextNote: Two points at 5 marks, and "differentiate" means the contrast has to be explicit. Three clean contrasts run through the scheme: endotoxins produced inside the cell against exotoxins produced outside it; easy to destroy against needing 30 minutes' boiling; symptoms after about 12 hours against within 2. Each option carries its own named bacteria, and mixing them up loses the point.

options: Infectious food poisoning - caused by consumption of food containing large numbers of pathogenic bacteria; these bacteria produce endotoxins as they grow, which are released when they die; endotoxins are easy to destroy; proper cooking and reheating will destroy both toxins and bacteria; if not destroyed symptoms will appear after approximately 12 hours; etc. Examples: salmonella, E coli, campylobacter; listeria; etc.

Toxic food poisoning - ingesting food that is contaminated by a toxin produced by a bacterial cell; some bacteria produce exotoxins as they grow in food both before and after it is eaten; exotoxins are hard to destroy; boiling for 30 mins is required; symptoms develop quickly, often within 2 hours; etc. Examples: staphylococcus aureus; clostridium botulinum; clostridium perfringens/welchii; etc.

notes: The two types kept whole, each with its mechanism, timing and examples, because the marks are in the comparison rather than in either description alone.

Three points at 2 marks - the biggest row. Production is a sequence from plant or animal to yarn, so tell it in order: where the fibre comes from, how it is harvested, how it is cleaned and separated, how it is spun. Read the option for the fabric you named.

options: Cotton Fibre production: comes from the boll or seed head of the cotton plant, with each fibre being between 2-3cm long; fibres are white and fluffy; the bolls are picked, by either hand or machine; the fibres are separated from the seeds; they are then pressed into bales; the cotton is then graded according to the length of the fibres; these fibres can be combed or spun into yarn

Linen Fibre production: made from the stem of the flax plant; flax stems are pulled and stems are retted, soaked until outer stem rots; stems are crushed and combed; fibres are spun into yarn; yarn is bleached and dyed; woven into a textured fabric

Wool Fibre production: comes from the soft hair / fleece of sheep, goats, llamas etc; fleece is removed/shorn from the animal; it is then collected and graded to the length of the fibres and also the colour and fineness of the wool; it is then cleaned and combed (carding); it is then spun into yarn and can then be used to produce textiles

Silk Fibre production: silkworm feeds on mulberry leaves; it spins a cocoon of silk around itself; cocoons are soaked in water; silk threads are unwound from cocoons onto reels; several of these thin silk threads are spun or twisted together to make thicker thread; these are then woven into fabric

Spread the four across spotting overspending, security, saving, and the skill itself.

options: alleviates worry and stress as bills will be paid
know where all monies are going
provides for emergencies e.g. visit to doctor or dentist
encourages people to wait until they have the money to buy something
ensures money available to cover unplanned eventualities e.g. job loss

notes: One flat list, taken in order to the cap.

questionText: Set out a weekly budget plan for a family (two adults and two children) with a net income of EUR 800 a week.
stem: Good money management is an important life skill.

rows.verbatim: Set out a weekly budget plan for a family with a net income of EUR 800 a week
rows.contextNote: Five points at 4 marks, graded 4:2:0. This is a plan, not prose: the scheme's percentages are the answer and a heading with its percentage earns the 4 where a heading alone earns 2. They total 100%, so the euro amounts have to add to EUR 800 — an arithmetic slip costs marks the headings had already earned. Reviewing the budget regularly is a point in its own right.

options: household bills 15% e.g. lighting, heating, bin collection, phone/internet
evaluate/review budget on a regular basis

notes: One flat list; the scheme's percentages are kept inside the options because they are the marking content.

questionText: State one advantage and one disadvantage of buying goods on credit.
stem: Good money management is an important life skill.

rows.verbatim: One advantage of buying goods on credit
rows.contextNote: One advantage, 5 marks. The question fixes one of each, so two advantages cannot score 10 however good they are. Graded 5:3:0 — stating it is 3, and explaining what it lets the buyer do is the 5.

options: have use of the goods without having to pay for them
no need to carry large sums of cash
can take advantage when sales are on
encourages spending and benefits the economy

rows.verbatim: One disadvantage of buying goods on credit
rows.contextNote: One disadvantage, 5 marks. The strongest are the ones with a consequence attached: goods can be repossessed if repayments are missed, and a poor credit rating makes future borrowing harder.

options: do not own goods until final instalment is paid
may be unable to keep up repayments
goods may be repossessed if consumer fails to meet repayments
consumer may get a poor credit rating/difficult to get a loan in the future.

notes: The question fixes one advantage and one disadvantage, so two rows rather than a pooled pair.

questionText: Describe each of the following family structures: one parent family; nuclear family; blended family.
stem: We live in an increasingly diverse world, even within our own family structures.

tariffModel.notation: one parent 2 points @ 3 marks (graded 3:2:0); nuclear 2 points @ 3 marks (graded 3:2:0); blended 2 points @ 3 marks (graded 3:2:0)

rows.contextNote: Two points at 3 marks. All three structures are compulsory and identically priced, so this is three short descriptions rather than a choice — skipping one costs a flat 6. Here the two points come easily as what it is and what follows from it: one parent with their children, and the financial or emotional pressures that can result.

options: consists of one parent and his/her child(ren), can be because of choice, divorce, separation, desertion or death of a spouse
can result in difficulties e.g. poverty, financial, emotional
stress due to increased workload and childcare problems
more likely to be dependent on state benefits

rows.contextNote: Two points at 3 marks. The scheme's description is longer than the others but the tariff is the same — parents and children in a self-contained unit, with shared tasks and small family size. Do not overspend on the structure you know best.

options: democratic, with older children involved in decision making
number of children is usually small

rows.contextNote: Two points at 3 marks. The definition is the first point — partners with children from previous relationships, often with children of their own — and the second is best taken from the consequences the scheme lists: extra financial pressure, or discipline between step-parents and children.

options: partners with children from previous relationships and often their own children
more common due to divorce and separation
difficulties with discipline between step-parents and children

notes: Three compulsory structures at 6 marks each, so three rows rather than a pooled choice.

questionText: Discuss the roles and responsibilities of adolescents/teenagers within a family.
stem: We live in an increasingly diverse world, even within our own family structures.

rows.verbatim: Discuss the roles and responsibilities of adolescents/teenagers within a family
rows.contextNote: Four points at 5 marks, graded 5:3:0. The scheme's strongest point is the tension it names outright: role expectations are difficult because an adolescent is no longer a child but does not yet carry the responsibility of an adult. Building an answer around that, rather than listing chores, is what reaches 5 a point.

options: role expectations are difficult as adolescents are no longer children but still do not have the full responsibility of adulthood
showing respect, learning to behave in a socially acceptable manner
to do a fair/appropriate share of household duties
to work hard and achieve in school
helping with minding younger siblings/elderly family members

notes: One flat list, taken in order to the cap.

questionText: Outline why good communication is important between family members.
stem: We live in an increasingly diverse world, even within our own family structures.

rows.verbatim: Outline why good communication is important between family members
rows.contextNote: Three points at 4 marks. Every entry has a consequence built into it — trust, resolved conflict, self-esteem, knowing what is expected — and naming the consequence is the second 2. "It is important to talk" is not a point; saying that clear expectations prevent conflict is.

options: family members know what is expected of them
able to express their opinions and views
helps members express opinions in a safe environment

notes: One flat list, evenly priced.

questionText: State four advantages of having a house well insulated.
stem: The diagram below shows the average heat loss for a family home. (www.ors.ie)

rows.verbatim: Advantages of a well insulated house
rows.contextNote: Four advantages at 5 marks, graded 5:3:0 - 20 marks, the biggest part here. The scheme runs three ways: money (lower bills), comfort (steady temperature, less noise), and environment (less energy used, lower CO2, better BER). Take from all three rather than saying "saves money" four ways.

options: reduces the use of energy resources
can contribute to sustainable and responsible living
higher BER rating/improvement in energy efficiency

notes: One flat list, taken in order to the cap.

questionText: Name and describe the method of insulation you would recommend for each of the following: attic; walls; windows.
stem: The diagram below shows the average heat loss for a family home. (www.ors.ie)

tariffModel.notation: Name 2 marks (graded 2:0) and description 3 marks (graded 3:0), x 3

rows.contextNote: Name and describe one, 5 marks. Blanket insulation is the one to know - rolls of fibreglass or mineral wool laid between the joists. Loose fill, foam and blown fibre are the alternatives.

options: blanket insulation e.g. rolls of fibreglass, wool or mineral
laid between joists or fixed between roof rafters
loose fill e.g. pellets of polystyrene or vermiculite poured in between joists
foam insulation e.g. foam sprayed between roof and rafters
blown- fibre insulation e.g. glass, mineral or cellulose fibres are blown into the attic and sealed

rows.contextNote: Name and describe one, 5 marks. Cavity wall is the classic: two layers of block 5-10cm apart with the air gap acting as the insulator, or foam and beads pumped into that cavity. Dry lining and external render are the alternatives for solid walls.

options: cavity walls: two layers of blocks, 5-10cm apart, air in the space acts as insulator
polystyrene sheets can be inserted at the building stage
polystyrene foam or beads are pumped into the cavity
internal solid walls: insulation sheets, dry lining applying insulating boards to the inside of external walls
external walls: sheets of insulating material to the outer surface of the wall and covered with a render to provide water resistance, a steel mesh is embedded in the render to provide strength

rows.contextNote: Name and describe one, 5 marks. Double or triple glazing - two or three sheets of glass with an air or argon gap. Low-emissivity glass reflects heat back into the room, and heavy lined curtains count too.

options: double or triple glaze: two/three sheets of glass with an air space between them, the space can be filled with an inert gas e.g. argon
low emissivity glass has an invisible coating that reduces heat transfer and reflects heat back into the room etc. curtains: heavy lined, fitted

notes: Fixed: three named areas of the house, priced identically at 5 marks each. Skipping one costs a straight 5.

questionText: State the advantages and/or the disadvantages of solar energy.
stem: The diagram below shows the average heat loss for a family home. (www.ors.ie)

rows.verbatim: Advantages and/or disadvantages of solar energy
rows.contextNote: Three points at 5 marks, graded 5:3:0. "And/or" means all three may come from one side, so you are not forced to balance them - but two advantages and one disadvantage reads as a fuller answer. The SEAI grant and the BER increase are the two most students forget.

options: provides a plentiful supply of hot water
SEAI grant available for cost of installing
increases the property value by raising the Building Energy Rating (BER)
undependable supply of sunshine, other form of energy required
house must be orientated towards the sun

notes: One flat list pooling both sides, because the question says "and/or" and the scheme prices three points across both.

questionText: State the advantages and the disadvantages of buying a home of your own.
stem: Buying a first home is an exciting adventure.

tariffModel.notation: 3 points @ 4 marks each (graded 4:2:0) - 1 advantage + 1 disadvantage + 1 other point

rows.verbatim: One advantage of buying a home
rows.contextNote: One advantage at 4 marks, and the scheme requires it. The strongest is that it is an investment with security of tenure - it is yours, and the value can rise.

options: less expensive, mortgage cheaper than renting
value of the house can increase
can choose your own design and type of house
whether to share house or not

rows.verbatim: One disadvantage of buying a home
rows.contextNote: One disadvantage at 4 marks, also required. The costs beyond the price are the real answer: deposit, legal fees, stamp duty, survey, property tax, and maintenance forever after.

options: additional fees to be paid e.g. lending agency, legal, stamp duty, buyer’s survey fee

rows.contextNote: One further point at 4 marks, from either side - "1 advantage + 1 disadvantage + 1 other point". Whichever list you found easier is where to take it from.

options: less expensive, mortgage cheaper than renting
value of the house can increase
can choose your own design and type of house
whether to share house or not
additional fees to be paid e.g. lending agency, legal, stamp duty, buyer’s survey fee

notes: Fixed: the scheme requires one point on each side, then floats the remaining 4 marks across both. Modelled as three rows so the two compulsory points cannot be lost.

questionText: Discuss how the housing requirements of a family with children may differ from that of a person living on their own.
stem: Buying a first home is an exciting adventure.

rows.contextNote: Three points at 6 marks, graded 6:3:0 - the highest per-point rate on the paper, so develop each one. The word is "differ", so write in contrasts: a family needs space, storage and a garden and wants to be near schools; someone on their own needs less space and can choose a location and lifestyle to suit only themselves.

options: depends on size and composition of family
older children like their own personal space
storage space e.g. lockers, wardrobes, hot press for clothes
well equipped, ventilated, adequately lit and spacious kitchen
enclosed garden, patio, decking for play
requires less space than a family
allows for individuals preference e.g. choosing between urban/rural lifestyle

notes: One flat list pooling both households, because the question asks how they differ and the scheme prices three points across both.

questionText: Discuss three factors to be considered when planning the interior design of a house.
stem: Interior designers help people create their dream home.

rows.contextNote: Three factors at 5 marks, graded 5:3:0. The scheme names them only, so the mark is in the sentence you add. Function of the room is the strongest - what happens in the room decides the flooring, the lighting and the furniture.

options: ergonomics, well laid out for ease of movement

notes: One flat list, taken in order to the cap.

questionText: Explain how soft furnishings can enhance the overall appearance of a room.
stem: Interior designers help people create their dream home.

rows.verbatim: How soft furnishings enhance a room
rows.contextNote: Three points at 5 marks, graded 5:3:0. Name the furnishing as well as the effect - cushions and a throw add colour and texture, curtains make a room warm and cosy, a rug can act as the focal point. The economical-makeover point is the one worth ending on.

options: make a room warm and cosy
act as a focal point in a room
add interest to an area of the room
can give a room a complete makeover in an economical way
can update style of a room

notes: One flat list, taken in order to the cap.

questionText: Suggest one accessory you could add to enhance an occasion wear outfit, and give one reason for your choice.
stem: ‘Fashions fade, style is eternal.’ (Yves Saint Laurent)

rows.contextNote: Name one, 3 marks, graded 3:0 - all or nothing, but any accessory in the list counts: a shawl, jewellery, a fascinator, cufflinks, a tie pin, a watch.

options: pashmina shawl in a contrasting pastel colour to add another layer to outfit
jewellery e.g. earrings, bracelet, necklace, rings, watch
tie in the same colour as the handkerchief

rows.contextNote: One reason at 4 marks - more than the accessory itself, so this is where the marks are. The scheme’s reasons are about how the piece works with the outfit: it adds a layer, it complements the suit, it picks up the colour of the handkerchief.

options: pashmina shawl in a contrasting pastel colour to add another layer to outfit
jewellery e.g. earrings, bracelet, necklace, rings, watch
tie in the same colour as the handkerchief

notes: Fixed: the accessory is priced at 3 and the reason at 4. Both rows draw on the same list, because the scheme prints each accessory together with the reason it works.

questionText: Write a profile of a natural fabric under each of the following headings: how the fabric is constructed; properties.
stem: Today’s consumers are willing to pay more for clothing produced with natural fabrics.

tariffModel.notation: construction 1 point @ 3 marks (graded 3:2:0); properties 2 points @ 3 marks each (graded 3:2:0)

rows.contextNote: One point at 3 marks. Weaving is the one the scheme explains properly - the warp runs down the loom, the weft passes over and under it, and the selvedge forms at the edges. Knitting and bonding are the shorter alternatives.

options: Weaving: is done on a loom; warp threads are stretched down the loom; weft threads are passed over and under the warp from one side to the other; as the weft threads come down the outside edges of the warp threads, a finishing edge called a selvedge edge is made
Knitting: can be done by hand or machine
Bonding: two or more fabrics are joined by adhesive; combination of a knit or loosely woven fabric backed by a lightweight lining

rows.contextNote: Two properties at 3 marks each - two thirds of the marks. Pick the fabric first, then take two from its own line. Include a weakness as well as a strength: linen is strong and cool but creases badly, wool is warm but shrinks and can itch.

options: Linen - absorbent; strong; conducts heat well; resists mildew; has a good lustre; may shrink; poor resistance to fire; little elasticity; soils easily; dyes well; creases easily
Cotton - absorbent; cool; strong; easy to wash and dry; dyes well; creases easily; shrinks
Wool - warm; soft; absorbent; resilient; can irritate sensitive skin; pills; shrinks
Silk - absorbent; crease resistant; drapes well; flammable; damaged by careless handling

notes: Fixed: construction is priced at 3 and the properties at 6. The properties row carries one option per fabric, because the two points must match whichever fabric was profiled.

questionText: Give two advantages of using natural fibres/fabric in everyday wear.
stem: Today’s consumers are willing to pay more for clothing produced with natural fabrics.

rows.verbatim: Advantages of natural fibres in everyday wear
rows.contextNote: Two advantages at 3 marks, graded 3:2:0. The scheme ties several to a specific fabric and use - wool is warm for winter, cotton absorbs sweat so it suits sportswear, linen is lightweight for summer. Naming the fabric with the advantage is what makes it a 3.

options: dyes easily so many colours available
wool is warm for winter clothing
cotton absorbs water so ideal for sportswear

notes: One flat list, taken in order to the cap.

questionText: Explain how each of the following factors may influence a person’s choice of clothing: function; money available; cultural influences.
stem: Irish fashion is thriving on the international stage.

rows.contextNote: One point, 3 marks. Function is what the clothing has to do - the scheme’s example is a waterproof coat in winter. Name an occasion or condition and the garment that suits it.

options: Particular garments are suitable for specific occasion e.g. waterproof coat in winter

rows.contextNote: One point, 3 marks. Budget decides where you shop as much as what you buy - designer, chain store or charity shop - and value for money over time is the point worth making.

options: Value for money in the long term
items chosen must fit into a low budget

rows.contextNote: One point, 3 marks. Modesty is the scheme’s main idea - different cultures cover differently - along with features borrowed between cultures, like pashminas, embroidery and beading.

options: Different cultures have different levels of modesty reflected in their clothing
features from different countries e.g. pashminas shawls, embroidery on t-shirts

notes: Fixed: the question names all three factors, so all three must be answered. Priced identically at 3 marks each.

questionText: Discuss the contribution of trendsetters/bloggers to current fashion trends.
stem: Irish fashion is thriving on the international stage.

rows.contextNote: Two contributions at 3 marks, graded 3:2:0. Say the mechanism - young people copy what trendsetters wear, brands sponsor celebrities and hand them clothes for media events, and social media spreads it in hours rather than seasons.

options: Young people want to wear what trendsetters are wearing
they set up their own clothing ranges
trendsetters are photographed wearing clothes by specific designers at media events
sponsorship deals that celebrities have with clothing companies
television programmes show confidence about clothing

notes: One flat list, taken in order to the cap.

questionText: Outline how education contributes to the development of the individual. Refer to each of the following: physical development; emotional development; intellectual development.
stem: Education for a child begins at home and is a lifelong process.

rows.contextNote: Two points at 3 marks. School builds the body two ways - fine motor skills through practical subjects and handling equipment, and gross motor skills, bone and muscle through PE and sport.

options: playing with toys helps with manual dexterity e.g. jigsaws
practical subjects can improve fine and gross motor skills
sport and physical education helps to build healthy bones and muscles and improve balance/fitness

rows.contextNote: Two points at 3 marks. Starting school is the first real independence from parents, and it is where children learn to notice and respond to how other people feel.

options: young children gain emotional independence from parents, encourages maturity
learn to be sensitive to needs of others
co-educational allows for development of healthy, friendly relationships between sexes

rows.contextNote: Two points at 3 marks, and the longest list. The range of subjects and the resources are the obvious ones; competition from classmates and the challenge of examinations are the ones that read as thought-out.

options: promoted through the wide range of subjects
resources e.g. books, computers assist development
home provides stimulation and nurtures a learning environment
comfortable physical surroundings with good lighting/heating and ventilation assist in attaining ones potential

notes: Fixed: the question names all three kinds of development and prices them identically at 6 marks each.

questionText: Give an account of four factors that influence the educational achievement of school children.
stem: Education for a child begins at home and is a lifelong process.

rows.contextNote: Four factors at 5 marks, graded 5:3:0 - 20 marks, the biggest part here. Say how the factor works, not just its name: a large family means financial strain and less one-to-one attention; the school environment covers resources, class size, SNAs and resource teachers.

options: family size, large family’s greater financial strain
peers, can be positive or negative
school environment e.g. resources in school, access to computers/assistive technology, SNA available to assist, resource teachers available
educational programmes in school e.g. JCSP, LCA, LCVP, TY, HEAR, DARE, RACE, level two learning programme, work experience

notes: One flat list, taken in order to the cap.

questionText: Explain three benefits to students of participating in work experience while in second level school.
stem: Education for a child begins at home and is a lifelong process.

rows.verbatim: Benefits of work experience to students
rows.contextNote: Three benefits at 4 marks, graded 4:2:0. The scheme splits into finding direction (deciding on a career, seeing what a job actually involves) and building skills (communication, teamwork, timekeeping, confidence). One from each is the fullest answer, and "it goes on your CV" is a legitimate third.

options: Helps students decide what career they may like to choose
gain knowledge of what actual working is like
get insight on what different jobs entail
get to know how people work together
see how work differs from school
realise what work activities are enjoyable
develop skills in communication, team working, planning, organising, timekeeping, problem solving
get the opportunity to take responsibility

notes: One flat list, taken in order to the cap.

questionText: Discuss three reasons why leisure is important in today’s society.
stem: ‘Physical activity plays an important role in the lives of children and young people.’ (www.education.ie)

rows.contextNote: Three reasons at 5 marks, graded 5:3:0. The scheme covers mind (relaxing, mental wellbeing, self-esteem), body (physical health) and people (social interaction, family bonding, community). One from each is the widest answer.

options: Helps people relax and unwind from stresses of daily life
sets good example for children on how to use their free time positively

notes: One flat list, taken in order to the cap.

questionText: Describe how a person’s choice of leisure activities are influenced by each of the following: cost; occupation; age.
stem: ‘Physical activity plays an important role in the lives of children and young people.’ (www.education.ie)

rows.contextNote: One point, 5 marks. It is not only the fee - equipment and special clothing cost too, and someone with less disposable income turns to activities that are free, like walking.

options: people with less disposable income may choose inexpensive/free activities e.g. walking

rows.contextNote: One point, 5 marks. The idea worth writing is contrast: someone sitting at a desk all day tends to choose something active, and someone doing physical work chooses something restful. Work also decides both the money and the hours available.

options: leisure can contrast with a person’s occupation
can be an extension of work
work is a means of providing income for leisure
part-time workers, job sharing and career breaks all allow for more time for leisure activities
sedentary worker could opt for an energy consuming type of activity and vice-versa

rows.contextNote: One point, 5 marks. Time and money move in opposite directions across a life - young people have time but little money, parents of small children have neither, and retired people have time again.

options: young people have fewer commitments and more time for leisure
couples with young children have the least amount of time and disposable income
retired people have more time and more disposable money to spend on leisure
older people have less money, may have physical constraints and do more sedentary pursuits
some leisure activities are considered too dangerous for children

notes: Fixed: the question names all three influences, so all three must be answered. Priced identically at 5 marks each.

questionText: Discuss the effects of unemployment on: young individuals; the family; society.
stem: The impact of unemployment can be long lasting.

rows.contextNote: Two points at 3 marks. The scheme goes further into the mind than the wallet - worthlessness, loss of identity and status, isolation, boredom, depression. Take one money point and one of those.
Two points at 3 marks. Keep it at household level: trouble paying rent and bills, strain on relationships, children suffering at school, and at worst losing the home.

options: provision of basic needs may be difficult
may become homeless or in need of emergency accommodation
children can suffer academically in school
may be tendency to turn to drink or drugs

rows.contextNote: Two points at 3 marks - the row most students leave thin. It is about cost and consequence to the country: benefits to pay, higher taxes, emigration, crime, and the cycle of poverty continuing.

options: burden on state to pay benefits
a growth in the black economy

notes: Fixed: three named strands, priced identically at 6 marks each. Answer all three - six good points about young people still scores 6.

questionText: Name and give details of one voluntary organisation that provides support to the unemployed.
stem: The impact of unemployment can be long lasting.

rows.contextNote: Name one, 4 marks, graded 4:0 - all or nothing, so give the organisation’s actual name. Seven are accepted, including Men’s Sheds, which students often overlook.

Two details at 4 marks - two thirds of the marks. The scheme prints one shared list rather than describing each body, so these apply to whichever you named: acting as a pressure group, informing government, funding classes that teach coping skills, and giving people a place to talk about their situation.

options: can offer government bodies detailed information and possible solutions
funding of classes to teach people the skills to help them cope with their situation
provide opportunity for people to discuss their situation

notes: Fixed: naming is priced at 4 and the details at 8. The scheme prints one set of details covering all the organisations rather than describing each, so the details row is a single shared list.

questionText: Give an account of the nutritive value and the dietetic value of eggs.
stem: The ultimate convenience food, eggs are powerhouses of nutrition. (www.bbcgoodfood.com)

tariffModel.notation: 5 points @ 4 marks each (graded 4:2:0) - 2 references to nutritive value, 2 references to dietetic value, plus 1 other

options: albumin, ovalbumin and globulin in white
fat soluble vitamins A, D, E and K

rows.contextNote: Two points at 4 marks, also required. Dietetic value is who it suits and why - easy to digest, quick to cook, ideal for growing children, and important in a vegetarian diet. Its weaknesses count too: no vitamin C, and the cholesterol.

options: used in sweet and savoury dishes
HBV protein for growth and repair
can be eaten on their own
a meal in themselves when served with toast for carbohydrate
important in the diet of a vegetarian

rows.verbatim: One further point, from either value
rows.contextNote: One further point at 4 marks, from either list - "2 references to nutritive value, 2 references to dietetic value, plus 1 other".

options: albumin, ovalbumin and globulin in white
fat soluble vitamins A, D, E and K

notes: Fixed: the scheme requires two points on each value, then floats the remaining 4 marks across both. Modelled as three rows so the four compulsory points cannot be lost.

questionText: Outline different ways of including eggs in the diet, and the effects of heat on eggs.
stem: The ultimate convenience food, eggs are powerhouses of nutrition. (www.bbcgoodfood.com)

tariffModel.notation: ways 3 @ 3 marks each; effects 3 @ 3 marks each (graded 3:2:0)

rows.verbatim: Ways of including eggs in the diet
rows.contextNote: Three ways at 3 marks. The scheme gives an example with every point, so use them - the mark comes from the dish, not the category. Work through the day: scrambled at breakfast, quiche at lunch, scotch eggs at dinner, meringue for dessert.

options: Eating on their own e.g. scrambled, fried, boiled, poached
lunch e.g. Quiche Lorraine, salads, frittata, omelettes, egg sandwich
dinner e.g. fish cakes, scotch eggs, Caesar salad
baked products e.g. scones, sponge cake
desserts e.g. custards, meringue, rice pudding

options: Protein coagulates causing eggs to solidify
overcooking makes them tough and difficult to digest
overcooking boiled eggs causes iron/sulphur ring around the yolk

questionText: Give three reasons for the growing popularity of goods supplied by small Irish food producers.
stem: The ultimate convenience food, eggs are powerhouses of nutrition. (www.bbcgoodfood.com)

rows.verbatim: Reasons for the popularity of small Irish food producers
rows.contextNote: Three reasons at 4 marks, graded 4:2:0. The scheme is short - quality and taste, organic production, local employment, and people willing to pay more for better. Say why each one draws the shopper in.

options: Foods healthier, more nutritious, and tastier
people willing to pay more for better quality

questionText: Discuss how the following might affect consumers’ decision making when shopping: household income; discount offers; shopper loyalty schemes.
stem: ‘Consumers want to hear about discounts and sales, not just products.’ (www.retail-week.com)

rows.contextNote: One point, 5 marks. When money is tight the order changes - needs before luxuries, and value for money becomes the deciding factor rather than preference.

options: amount of money available for spending
when disposable income is limited consumers must ensure needs are met before luxuries are purchased
try to get good value for money

rows.contextNote: One point, 5 marks. The scheme is blunt about it: offers create the impression of a bargain and push impulse buying, so people end up spending more, not less.

options: persuade the consumer to impulse buy
special offers give the impression of extra bargains

rows.contextNote: One point, 5 marks, and the longest list. Points and perks build an emotional tie to one shop, which is exactly the point - a loyal shopper stops comparing prices elsewhere.

options: offer consumers perks and rewards for their continued shopping
encourage consumer loyalty to the one supermarket
build an emotional connection to a particular shop
build on loyalty to a particular brand
loyalty cards offer discounts, invitation to sale preview
less chance of shopping around for best value for money

questionText: State the advantages and the disadvantages of online shopping.
stem: ‘Consumers want to hear about discounts and sales, not just products.’ (www.retail-week.com)

tariffModel.notation: 3 points @ 5 marks each (graded 5:3:0) - 1 advantage, 1 disadvantage, plus 1 other

rows.contextNote: One advantage at 5 marks, and the scheme requires it. Convenience is the heart of it - no need to leave home, no opening hours, and you can compare across sites and read reviews before buying.

options: Do not have to leave home
not restricted by opening hours, goods may be purchased anytime

rows.contextNote: One disadvantage at 5 marks, also required. Not being able to touch or try the goods is the main one, along with the risks - fraud, sites that are not legitimate, and the cost and hassle of returning things.

options: lack of touch and feel of merchandise
lack of interactivity with shop assistant
